user_query: Identify the top three product categories whose most commonly used payment type has the highest number of payments across all categories, and specify the number of payments made in each category using that payment type.
clean_summary: Changing the aggregation to `COUNT(DISTINCT p.order_id)` fixes overcounting of multiple payment records per order, producing the correct distinct order counts per category.
database_memories: ENSURE: when aggregating the number of orders in the payments table, use COUNT(DISTINCT payments.order_id) instead of COUNT(*) to count unique orders | CONTEXT: the payments table stores one row per payment transaction with payments.order_id as the link to each order, so COUNT(*) will overcount orders with multiple payment records | WHEN_TO_CHECK: when computing payment counts per grouping (for example, per product category) by querying the payments table | EXAMPLE_USAGE:
JOIN products pr ON p.product_id = pr.product_id
SELECT pr.category_id, COUNT(DISTINCT p.order_id) AS payment_count
JOIN products pr ON p.product_id = pr.product_id
generic_memories: VERIFY: aggregation of unique entities in a fact table uses COUNT(DISTINCT key) rather than COUNT(*) | PRINCIPLE: COUNT(*) counts all rows including duplicates from one-to-many relationships, whereas COUNT(DISTINCT key) ensures each unique entity is counted only once | WHEN_TO_APPLY: whenever counting distinct items (such as orders, customers, or sessions) from tables that can contain multiple records per item | EXAMPLE_USAGE:
Situation: you have an events table where each session generates multiple event rows.
SELECT COUNT(*) AS session_count FROM events;
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT session_id) AS session_count FROM events;

index_rows.applies_when: when computing payment counts per grouping
index_rows.rule:
ENSURE: when aggregating the number of orders in the payments table, use COUNT(DISTINCT payments.order_id) instead of COUNT(*) to count unique orders | CONTEXT: the payments table stores one row per payment transaction with payments.order_id as the link to each order, so COUNT(*) will overcount orders with multiple payment records | WHEN_TO_CHECK: when computing payment counts per grouping (for example, per product category) by querying the payments table | EXAMPLE_USAGE:
Incorrect:
SELECT pr.category_id, COUNT(*) AS payment_count
FROM payments p
JOIN products pr ON p.product_id = pr.product_id
GROUP BY pr.category_id;
Correct:
SELECT pr.category_id, COUNT(DISTINCT p.order_id) AS payment_count
FROM payments p
JOIN products pr ON p.product_id = pr.product_id
GROUP BY pr.category_id;

VERIFY: aggregation of unique entities in a fact table uses COUNT(DISTINCT key) rather than COUNT(*) | PRINCIPLE: COUNT(*) counts all rows including duplicates from one-to-many relationships, whereas COUNT(DISTINCT key) ensures each unique entity is counted only once | WHEN_TO_APPLY: whenever counting distinct items (such as orders, customers, or sessions) from tables that can contain multiple records per item | EXAMPLE_USAGE:
Situation: you have an events table where each session generates multiple event rows.
Incorrect:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS session_count FROM events;
(This counts every event row.)
Correct:
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT session_id) AS session_count FROM events;
(This counts each session exactly once.)
